title: Student-Teacher Curriculum Learning via Reinforcement Learning: Predicting Hospital Inpatient Admission Location
venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to improve neural network training by using a teacher-student curriculum learning framework, with the immediate application of predicting hospital inpatient admission location from emergency department triage data. The authors frame training as a reinforcement learning problem in which a teacher network learns to select which batch of training data the student network should see next, based on the student’s current state.

The proposed approach uses the student’s network weights as the teacher’s state representation. Training data are first ordered into a curriculum by an entropy-like measure: for tabular clinical data, Mahalanobis distance after autoencoder encoding; for CIFAR-10, cosine similarity. The teacher then chooses the center and width of each batch, with reward defined by the student’s improvement in accuracy on both training and validation sets, which is intended to reduce overfitting and steer the student through easier-to-harder or otherwise task-appropriate curricula.

The empirical context includes hospital electronic health record data from an Oxford hospital trust (ward admission prediction), MIMIC-III ICU data (mortality prediction), and CIFAR-10 as a non-medical benchmark. The paper reports that the reinforcement-learning-based teacher-student method outperforms simpler batchwise and fixed curriculum baselines, and is competitive with or better than several tabular and image-classification methods. The learned policies often exhibit structured behaviors such as entropy spiking, gradual entropy progression, and transfer across related tasks, suggesting that the teacher can learn stable and task-sensitive curricula from the student’s evolving state.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A teacher-student curriculum learning framework in which a higher-level teacher agent selects training data batches for a student model based on the student’s state and reward feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a reinforcement-learning-based curriculum learning method for training predictive neural networks, not as a K-12 instructional product.

findings.finding_summary: The proposed student-teacher curriculum learning method improved classification performance over batchwise training, vanilla curriculum training, and prior student-teacher curriculum learning baselines on the ward admission task. On the ward admission dataset, the DDPG student-teacher achieved 0.62 (SD 0.02) accuracy versus 0.45 (0.01) for batchwise training and 0.48 (0.02) for curriculum training (n=14,324 total patients; 8,589 training patients).
findings.measure: Classification accuracy on ward admission prediction

findings.finding_summary: On the MIMIC-III mortality prediction task, the DDPG student-teacher achieved 0.70 (SD 0.01) accuracy, outperforming batchwise training (0.63, SD 0.01), vanilla curriculum training (0.63, SD 0.02), and the DQN student-teacher baseline (0.66, SD 0.02). The study reports the dataset contained 8,806 patients and used a train/validation/test split of 60/20/20.
findings.measure: Classification accuracy on MIMIC-III mortality prediction

findings.finding_summary: On CIFAR-10, the DDPG student-teacher reached 0.90 (SD 0.01) on sample 1 and 0.90 (SD 0.01) on sample 2, exceeding batchwise training (0.65, SD 0.02) and vanilla curriculum training (0.68, SD 0.01) as well as the DQN student-teacher (0.86, SD 0.04; 0.88, SD 0.02). The paper evaluates three sampled CIFAR-10 test sets and reports competitive performance relative to image-classification baselines.
findings.sample_size: n=12,000 training images sampled; n=3,000 test images sampled per run

quality_tier_rationale: This is not an empirical K-12 education study and does not evaluate an instructional AI tool in classrooms. It is a machine learning methods paper about reinforcement-learning-based curriculum training for hospital prediction and image classification.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct K-12 instructional or coaching impact, and no evidence about teacher support, lesson feedback, or student learning in education settings. Its reported effects are limited to classification accuracy in non-educational tasks.
